member.name: T:ktsu.Semantics.Quantities.NormalizedParameter`1
member.summary: Maps a host-normalized parameter position in [0, 1] onto a real value range, and back, using a configurable .
member.remarks: Plugin hosts automate parameters as a normalized [0, 1] value, but a control's useful range is rarely linear in that domain — frequency and gain feel right on a logarithmic taper, while many controls want extra resolution at one end. centralises that mapping so an effect parameter can declare its range and taper once and convert in both directions: turns the host's [0, 1] into the real value, and turns a real value back into [0, 1] for the host. Construct instances with the factory methods rather than .

member.name: T:ktsu.Semantics.Quantities.QFactor`1
member.summary: Represents the quality factor (Q) of a resonant filter or EQ band.
member.remarks: Q is the dimensionless ratio of a filter's centre frequency to its bandwidth: a higher Q means a narrower, more resonant response. member.name: T:ktsu.Semantics.Quantities.IUnit
member.summary: Common surface for every physical unit. Carries the unit's name, symbol, the it belongs to, and the affine conversion (base = value × ToBaseFactor + ToBaseOffset) that maps values in this unit to the SI base unit of the dimension.

remarks.para: For dimensional compile-time safety, generated quantity types do not accept the raw on In(...). Each dimension has its own marker interface (e.g. ILengthUnit : IUnit) which only its units implement, and the generated In(I<Dim>Unit) overload accepts only that family. So length.In(Units.Kilogram) fails to compile.
ToBase / FromBase are default-implemented; concrete units only have to provide and .

The conversion itself reads and , not the properties. Their default implementations convert those properties, so a unit written outside this library behaves as it always did. The generated units override them with the factor materialised directly into the storage type, which is what gives a quantity all 28 of its digits.

member.name: T:ktsu.Semantics.Quantities.PhysicalQuantityCore
member.summary: The validity and cross-dimension comparison rules every generated physical quantity shares.
member.remarks: These used to be inherited from an abstract PhysicalQuantity record. Generated quantities are structs now, and a struct cannot inherit, so each one declares the three members and delegates here — three one-line bodies per type instead of a copy of the rule. The receiver is taken by and constrained to a struct so that delegating does not box it; only the argument, which is already an interface at the call site, can be boxed.

member.name: M:ktsu.Semantics.Quantities.PhysicalQuantityCore.Compare``2(``0@,ktsu.Semantics.Quantities.IPhysicalQuantity{``1})
member.summary: Compares to another quantity of the same physical dimension.
member.remarks: Quantities of different dimensions are not ordered, so this throws rather than inventing an answer. Equality, below, is total instead and returns .
member.typeparam: The storage type for the quantity value.
member.param: The quantity to compare against, or .
member.returns: A negative number, zero or a positive number as sorts before, with, or after . A other sorts first.
member.exception: When the two quantities do not share a physical dimension.

member.summary: Reports whether two quantities share a dimension and a value.
member.remarks: Equality is total: comparing across dimensions returns rather than throwing, because a collection asking whether it already holds a value must get an answer.
member.typeparam: The storage type for the quantity value.
member.param: The quantity to compare against, or .

member.name: T:ktsu.Semantics.Quantities.StorageLiteral
member.summary: Materialises a metadata literal into a storage type at that type's own precision, for the conversion factors and metric magnitudes the generated code caches per closed generic type.

remarks.para: A factor used to reach a storage type through T.CreateChecked(double), so every type inherited the rounding of , and kept only the 15 significant digits that conversion preserves. Parsing the literal gives each type the nearest value it can represent, and a fraction is divided in the storage type itself.

Both methods answer when a storage type keeps the old route, and the generated holder then converts the constant with T.CreateChecked each time the value is read. An integer type keeps it, because parsing "0.3048" into an fails, and dividing 5 by 9 in one answers zero for a different reason than truncating 0.5555… does. A type that cannot parse the literal keeps it too.

Nothing here converts the , and that is deliberate. The generated holder evaluates every value for a storage type in one static initializer, so a conversion that overflowed there, such as 10^12 into , would make every value for that type throw , which is what 5.2.0 shipped. Converting at the read lets each value succeed or throw on its own, as the generated factories did before 5.2.0.

member.name: M:ktsu.Semantics.Quantities.StorageLiteral.Parse``1(System.String)
member.summary: Parses a decimal literal into .
member.param: The literal as written in the metadata, for example "0.3048" or "1e-10".
member.returns: The nearest value represents, or when is an integer or cannot parse the literal.

member.name: M:ktsu.Semantics.Quantities.StorageLiteral.Divide``1(System.String,System.String)
member.summary: Divides one decimal literal by another in .
member.returns: The quotient at the precision divides to, or when is an integer, cannot parse either literal, or overflows dividing them.

member.summary: Parses a literal with , treating a parse that throws for that style the same as one that returns .
member.param: The parsed value, or the default when parsing failed.
member.remarks: A numeric type outside the base library may throw or for a style it does not handle, rather than return . Only those two are caught, so any other failure still surfaces.

member.returns: when one divided by two is zero in .

member.name: T:ktsu.Semantics.Quantities.StorageMath
member.summary: Numeric operations the generated quantities need that does not declare.

member.name: F:ktsu.Semantics.Quantities.StorageMath.MaximumIterations
member.summary: The most Newton steps taken before the root is reported as not converging.
member.remarks: The seed is always within a factor of two of the root, and from there each step roughly doubles the number of correct digits, so a type would need far more digits than any real one holds to come near the cap. Reaching it means the estimate is cycling rather than settling, and the estimate at that point is not the root, so it is an error rather than an answer.

member.name: M:ktsu.Semantics.Quantities.StorageMath.Sqrt``1(``0)
member.summary: Computes the square root of a storage value at the precision of its type.
member.param: The value to take the root of. Generated callers pass a sum of squares, which is never negative.
member.returns: The square root of , or its floor for an integer type.
member.exception: is negative and cannot represent the that results.
The Newton steps do not settle on a root within .

remarks.para: The binary floating point and integer primitives take the route every generated Length() and Distance() took before this helper existed, a round trip through , so their results are unchanged. For them that route is already as precise as the type.

Any other type is refined in its own arithmetic: seeded near the root, then Newton steps x = (x + value / x) / 2 until the estimate stops changing. A root therefore has 28 significant digits rather than the 15 its conversion from keeps, and no constraint beyond is needed, which could not meet had this required .
A negative input keeps its old behaviour too, where the type has one and an exception where it does not.

member.name: M:ktsu.Semantics.Quantities.StorageMath.IsRoundedThroughDouble``1
member.summary: Reports whether is one of the primitives whose square root has always been taken through .
member.returns: for the binary floating point and integer primitives.
member.remarks: Written as comparisons because the JIT folds them for a value type, so each specialisation of compiles down to one of its two branches.

member.name: M:ktsu.Semantics.Quantities.StorageMath.Seed``1(``0,``0)
member.summary: Chooses the first Newton estimate for a positive value.
member.param: The positive value whose root is wanted.
member.returns: An estimate within a factor of two of the root.

remarks.para: The root is used directly when converts to a normal . Otherwise the value is outside the range of , or too small for a to hold with any precision, or the type does not convert at all. It is then scaled by powers of four into [1, 4), which every type holds, the root is taken there, and that root is scaled back by the matching power of two.

This used to start from the value itself. Newton's method still converges from there, but each early step only halves the estimate, so a of 2^2048 used every step on halving and returned about 2^1792 as its root.

member.name: M:ktsu.Semantics.Quantities.StorageMath.TryRootThroughDouble``1(``0,``0@)
member.summary: Takes the root of a value through when the value converts to a normal and the root converts back to something other than zero.
member.param: The root in , or the default when this fails.

member.name: T:ktsu.Semantics.Quantities.Vector0Guards
member.summary: Runtime guards used by generated quantity types to enforce the non-negativity invariant declared in the unified-vector model.
member.remarks:
Per the locked design decisions in docs/strategy-unified-vector-quantities.md:
A Vector0 quantity is always non-negative. Construction with a negative value throws .
The conversion from a non-base unit can flip the sign (e.g. -460°F is below absolute zero in Kelvin); the guard runs after conversion to catch that.

member.name: M:ktsu.Semantics.Quantities.Vector0Guards.EnsurePositive``1(``0,System.String)
member.summary: Returns unchanged when it is strictly positive; throws otherwise. Used in generated From{Unit} factories on V0 overloads that declare physicalConstraints.minExclusive: "0" in dimensions.json (per #51). member.name: T:ktsu.Semantics.Quantities.SoundPressureLevel`1
member.summary: Represents a sound pressure level (SPL) in decibels relative to the 20 µPa threshold of hearing.
member.remarks: SPL is a logarithmic field quantity: SPL = 20·log10(p / p₀) with p₀ = 20 µPa. Logarithmic scales don't obey linear arithmetic, so this type is generated as a standalone companion (from logarithmic.json) rather than a physical dimension.
